claims.text: The starting feedstock is cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder prepared by conventional powder-metallurgy routes.
Binder jetting or 3D ink-extrusion can shape a binder-containing green body at ambient temperature and subsequently densify it by isothermal sintering.
Binder jetting followed by optimized isothermal sintering will improve the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi relative to conventional fabrication.
The proposed route eliminates the high thermal gradients associated with conventional melt-based fabrication.
High thermal gradients in conventional melt-based fabrication cause compositional segregation.
High thermal gradients in conventional melt-based fabrication cause residual thermal stress and defect formation.
Sintering AlCrFeNiSi at approximately 1000–1200 °C is sufficient to achieve full elemental interdiffusion.
Slow cooling after sintering minimizes residual stress in AlCrFeNiSi parts.
Full interdiffusion during isothermal sintering promotes a segregation-free, structurally homogeneous microstructure.
Isothermal sintering can produce parts with low residual stress.
The proposed route reduces porosity and produces higher-density AlCrFeNiSi parts.
Ambient-temperature shaping avoids the high cooling rates and localized overheating typical of fusion-based processes.
Subsequent isothermal sintering provides densification and full interdiffusion.
Controlled isothermal sintering significantly reduces defects and produces a uniform grain structure.
The proposed route produces a more homogeneous elemental distribution than conventional bulk or laser-based additive manufacturing.
The proposed route improves strength and toughness relative to conventional fabrication.
Laser melting and furnace sintering of pressed powders exhibit noticeable segregation, higher residual stress, and increased defect formation.
Applicability to very complex geometries or extreme component sizes remains unconfirmed.
Prolonged isothermal exposure may produce minor secondary phases in AlCrFeNiSi.
